topic: First impressions take a tenth of a second, not 7 seconds
title: Do First Impressions Form in a Tenth of a Second?
voiceover: Do first impressions really form in a tenth of a second? In 2006, Janine Willis and Alexander Todorov showed people unfamiliar faces for just 100 milliseconds. Other people saw the faces for 500 milliseconds or a full second. They rated traits like trustworthiness and competence. Judgments after 100 milliseconds correlated with judgments made with no time limit. Extra viewing time did not significantly raise that correlation. It did make people more confident in their ratings. Judgments were also more negative at 500 milliseconds than at 100. Agreement between ratings is not accuracy, and the study did not test whether the faces really had those traits. So snap judgments form fast, but this study doesn't show they're right. Tomorrow: do a teacher's expectations change how students perform?

description: Do we judge faces in 100 milliseconds? A 2006 study found snap judgments correlated with judgments made with no time limit, but correlation is not accuracy. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Willis, J., & Todorov, A. (2006). First impressions: Making up your mind after a 100-ms exposure to a face. Psychological Science, 17(7), 592-598.
accuracy_note: Willis & Todorov (2006) measured agreement between quick and unlimited-time ratings, not whether the ratings were accurate. The popular '7 seconds' figure was not checked and is not used.
